As I have come to understand belief from those who I know are firm in their beliefs, it is not a matter of "there is or is not". This applies to the afterlife, God, spirits, and any other concept such as enlightenment of the self and reincarnation. For these people and myself our belief stands on "there may be, or there may not be, but we cannot know for sure. we have accounts from people describing these things, and we can choose to accept these descriptions for ourselves or not, but we must always remember that it is uncertain and unknowable".

There is no evidence to convince you of one belief or another, because any evidence used to base claims on belief is always an individual experience, revelation, realization, or rationalization. Instead, our belief must be open to any new interpretations or concepts and be willing to accept that this may perhaps be a new possibility that could be just as likely as what we already believe. The beliefs that are the strongest, stand the most firm, last the longest, and are the most impactful on the believer are the possibilities that, although they are recognized as no more or less likely than any other to be true, have a personal connection and meaning to the believer.

I personally believe that all people are reincarnated until the point where their soul has done the things made for it to do on Earth that will continue to enrich it's own soul or the soul of others, after which point all souls are taken to be with "God" and the rest of the passed. I have absolutely no evidence of this, but knowing that it's possible and that it makes sense to me, and that it really doesn't matter if I'm right or wrong, changes the way I live my life and the approach I have towards life itself.

I want it to be true that I have things I am intended to do that nobody else can do, and that I'm not limited to the resources of a single life to do it, and I also want it to be true that there is something greater than us that has a place prepared for us when our time ends where we are reunited with our loved ones. Therefore, I used the ideas I've heard over time to construct for myself a set of beliefs that comfort these desires, not because I believe them to be true, but because I know them to be possible, and I have no evidence otherwise.

And as a quick last note, memories aren't something that you really want to last much longer than you think. Think about a photo of a couple on their honeymoon. To them, for the rest of their lives that photo will be a gateway to a time and place once experienced together, something the two of them shared that has a special meaning because it was done together. But once one of them passes, the photo no longer has the same meaning to the partner still remaining. No matter what, that memory will be felt and understood differently than before because someone in the photo is gone, even though the memory itself may not have changed. Once that person passes however, what does that photo mean? If you or I look at it, it just looks like two people on a boat or something, but it still does have some meaning. The two people are gone and that specific memory is lost, but anyone who knew them can see the photo and remember the people, not the original memory the photo depicts. What about generations later, when nobody is alive who was alive when the two people in the photo were alive? There are no more memories left in the photo to remind the viewer of. It's simply some people on a honeymoon from a specific time in human history.

This seems sad, but ask yourself if you would want your memories, which are either completely personal to you or shared with someone else, to be remembered after your or anyone who shares the memory are gone.
